abstract.t: This specification defines two lifecycle commands that an Identity Service can send to a Relying Party (RP) to manage federated session lifecycle: Reestablish Session and Invalidate Access. These commands provide the Identity Service with on-demand control over RP session validity and authentication artifact acceptance, enabling access revalidation and security containment across federated systems. They do not affect authorization policy (roles, permissions, or entitlements) within the RP.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: In federated single sign-on deployments, an Identity Service authenticates subjects and issues assertions to Relying Parties (RPs). Once a session is established at the RP, the RP operates independently — it may continue accepting that session long after conditions at the Identity Service have changed. This creates a gap: the Identity Service has no reliable way to require the RP to stop relying on a prior authentication and check back before allowing continued access.

This specification closes that gap by defining two lifecycle commands through which the Identity Service exercises its role as Session Authority (see Section 2) over sessions derived from its assertions:
These commands affect session validity and the continued acceptability of prior authentication artifacts. They do not affect roles, permissions, entitlements, or authorization policy within the RP.

texttable.c: All RP client sessions for the subject
Policy change, risk signal, logout, session management
All sessions, tokens, and API keys

section.name: IPSIE Session Lifecycle Levels
section.t: The commands enable progressively greater Identity Service control over RP sessions. The following table summarizes what each level requires:

texttable.c: Time-based only. RP expires session when assertion validity period ends or timeout occurs
None. Identity Service sets session lifetime via assertion claims (exp, NotOnOrAfter)
Time-based and on-demand. Identity Service can require session reestablishment or full authentication state invalidation at any time
Direct. Identity Service sends Reestablish Session and Invalidate Access commands to RP
Time-based, on-demand, and continuous. RP and Identity Service exchange state changes in real time via Shared Signals
Continuous. Bidirectional communication of session, device, and risk state changes via CAEP/SSF
Both SL2 commands (REQUIRED) + continuous access signals

section.t: SL2 conformance requires that:

list.t: The Identity Service MUST be able to send both Reestablish Session and Invalidate Access commands to the Application
The Application MUST process and enforce both commands as defined in this specification
The Application MUST NOT accept unsolicited federation assertions (e.g., SAML IdP-initiated SSO)
The Identity Service MUST enforce authentication method requests from the Application

section.t: SL3 conformance builds on SL2 and additionally requires bidirectional state communication via Shared Signals (CAEP), enabling continuous access evaluation.

section.name: Notation and Conventions
section.t: The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY, and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in .

section.name: Terminology
section.t: Authentication The process of verifying the identity of a subject (user, device, or workload). §4

Authentication State The collection of artifacts that together represent the outcome of a successful authentication event and allow a subject to continue accessing resources without reauthenticating. Authentication state includes the RP client session, access tokens, refresh tokens, and API keys that were established or issued as a result of the subject's authentication. Authentication state is scoped to a subject at a specific RP and is distinct from authorization state (roles, permissions, entitlements). In this specification, the Invalidate Access command requires the RP to treat all of these artifacts as no longer valid. §7 (session management), §6 (assertion lifetime and protection), §1.4, §1.5 (token lifecycle)

Authorization The process of determining what actions or resources an authenticated subject is permitted to access. Authorization is distinct from authentication and is not affected by the commands defined in this specification. §1.1

Access Token A credential issued by an Authorization Server that represents the authorization granted to a client to access protected resources at a Resource Server. Access tokens have a limited lifetime and may be self-contained (e.g., JWT) or reference-based. §1.4

API Key A long-lived, static credential issued by the RP (not the Authorization Server) that grants API access to the RP's resources on behalf of a subject. API keys include service keys, personal access tokens (PATs), and static bearer tokens. Unlike OAuth tokens, API keys are typically not bound to an OAuth grant, are not rotated via refresh tokens, and may have no expiration. API keys are authentication artifacts and are within the scope of the Invalidate Access command.

Assertion A statement from an Identity Provider to a Relying Party that conveys information about an authentication event and the authenticated subject. In OIDC, the ID Token serves as the assertion; in SAML, the <Assertion> element. §4, §2, §2.3
Authorization Server (AS) The server that issues access tokens and refresh tokens to a client after successfully authenticating the resource owner and obtaining authorization. §1.1

Expire To end the validity of an artifact (session, token, assertion) so that it is no longer accepted. Expiration may occur naturally when a time-based validity period ends (e.g., an assertion's exp claim at SL1). Expiration is a normal lifecycle event, not an indication of a security incident. §1.5, §3.1.3.7 (exp claim)

Session Authority The Identity Service that issued the original assertion establishing the subject's session at the RP. The session authority is fixed at the time the session is established and cannot change while the session is Active, Expired, or Invalid. As session authority, the Identity Service retains the right to require the RP to revalidate or terminate sessions derived from its assertions, which is the role that the commands defined in this specification exercise. When a subject authenticates via federation, the RP records the session authority's issuer identifier and the subject's identifier (sub in OIDC; NameID in SAML), and optionally the session identifier (sid). These values identify which Identity Service is the session authority for the subject and enable the RP to redirect the subject directly to the correct Identity Service without requiring IdP discovery. The session authority is cleared when the session is Terminated, at which point the subject may select a different Identity Service (if available) when establishing a new session. §2 (iss, sub, sid), §2.4

Identity Provider (IdP) The entity that authenticates subjects and issues assertions to Relying Parties. Also referred to as OpenID Provider (OP) in OIDC and Identity Provider (IdP) in SAML. §1.2, §2.2

Forced Reauthentication An authentication intent in which the RP explicitly requires a fresh authentication event at the IdP, regardless of any existing IdP authentication session. The existing session MUST NOT be reused. The IdP MUST require a new primary authentication ceremony, the resulting authentication context MUST have a new auth_time, and previous authentication context values MUST NOT be relied upon. Both the Reestablish Session and Invalidate Access commands require the RP to trigger Forced Reauthentication. See Section 3 for the full definition of authentication intents. §7.2

Session Continuation An authentication intent in which the RP requests authentication and the IdP determines that an existing authentication session satisfies the RP's stated authentication freshness and assurance requirements. No new authentication event occurs. The IdP reuses the existing session and its authentication context (auth_time, acr, amr). Session Continuation is the normal flow when the RP needs to reestablish local application state (e.g., after local session expiry, cookie loss, or RP-local logout) without requiring fresh authentication. See Section 3 for the full definition of authentication intents. §5.3

Step-Up Authentication An authentication intent in which the RP requires a higher level of assurance than is provided by the existing authentication session. The IdP evaluates whether the current authentication context satisfies the requested assurance and, if insufficient, requires additional authentication. The resulting authentication context reflects the updated assurance, including updated acr, amr, and auth_time as appropriate. See Section 3 for the full definition of authentication intents. §7.2

User Presence An authentication intent in which the RP requires the subject to actively confirm they are present at the session, without requiring a full primary authentication ceremony or elevated assurance. The subject performs a lightweight presence gesture such as touching a security key, completing a biometric scan, entering a PIN, or acknowledging a push notification. The RP signals this intent by requesting acr_values="urn:ipsie:acr:presence" (OIDC) or an equivalent AuthnContextClassRef (SAML). The returned acr MUST equal urn:ipsie:acr:presence and auth_time MUST reflect the time of the presence confirmation. The amr claim reflects the specific gesture performed. See Section 3 for the full definition of authentication intents. §7.2

Refresh Token A credential issued by an Authorization Server that a client uses to obtain new access tokens without requiring the resource owner to reauthenticate. Refresh tokens are typically long-lived and revocable. §1.5

Relying Party (RP) The application or service that depends on the Identity Provider for authentication of subjects. Also referred to as Service Provider (SP) in SAML or Client in OAuth. §1.2, §2.2, §4
Resource Server (RS) The server hosting protected resources, capable of accepting and responding to requests using access tokens. §1.1

Invalidate To render an artifact (token, session, API key, or authentication state) no longer valid or trustworthy, regardless of its remaining lifetime. Invalidation is an active security operation, typically in response to a security event. In this specification, "Invalidate Access" denotes the Identity Service-initiated command to invalidate all prior authentication artifacts for a subject. §7.1

Logout An explicit action that terminates a subject's authenticated session at the RP, transitions the session to the Terminated state, and requires Forced Reauthentication before the subject can regain interactive access. Logout is distinct from time-based session expiry (which may allow Session Continuation) and from the Reestablish Session command (which expires the session without terminating it). Common forms include:

list.t: User-Initiated Logout: The subject explicitly requests to end their session (e.g., by clicking "Sign Out"). The RP session is terminated. OAuth access tokens, refresh tokens, and API keys are typically preserved, as the subject may have active background processes. The IdP SSO session MAY be terminated depending on whether the logout is propagated to the Identity Service via OIDC Logout or SAML SLO.

Admin-Initiated Logout: An administrator explicitly terminates the subject's session via a management portal or administrative action. The RP session is terminated. OAuth tokens and API keys MAY be preserved or revoked depending on administrative policy. The IdP SSO session SHOULD be terminated.

Policy or System-Initiated Logout: The Identity Service or RP terminates a session based on automated policy (e.g., idle timeout enforcement, compliance policy, device posture failure) rather than a direct user or admin action. Artifact scope depends on the policy that triggered the logout.

section.t: In all cases, the subject must re-authenticate through the Identity Service before regaining interactive access. This re-authentication gives the Identity Service an opportunity to re-evaluate policy, risk, and account state before issuing a new assertion, the same access-revalidation opportunity provided by the Reestablish Session command. See Section 5.2 for how Logout protocols (OIDC Back-Channel Logout, OIDC Front-Channel Logout, SAML SLO) satisfy the Reestablish Session command contract.

Revoke / Revocation The act of explicitly canceling a specific credential or token before its natural expiration, rendering it permanently unusable. Revocation is a specific form of invalidation applied to individual artifacts. §1

Session A temporary, stateful security context that is established after a successful authentication event and allows a subject to continue accessing a system without reauthenticating for each request. Sessions are time-limited, context-bound, and revocable. §7, §15.5.1

Single Sign-On (SSO) A mechanism that allows a subject to authenticate once at an Identity Provider and subsequently access multiple Relying Parties without reauthenticating at each one, for the duration of the IdP session. §5.3
Subject The entity (user, device, or workload) whose identity is asserted by the Identity Provider. §2 (sub claim), §2.4

section.name: Federated Session Lifecycle
section.t: The Reestablish Session and Invalidate Access commands, together with Logout, affect RP session and authentication state in distinct ways. Logout terminates the session while preserving tokens. Reestablish Session marks the session Invalid while preserving tokens. Invalidate Access terminates the session and invalidates all artifacts. This section defines a logical model for the lifecycle of a federated authentication session at the Relying Party. The model provides a framework for understanding how each command transitions the subject's state. It describes the states and transitions of RP session and authentication-artifact state. It does not model RP subscriber account lifecycle (e.g., provisioning, disabling, or deleting accounts), which is addressed separately by the IPSIE Account Lifecycle (AL) levels.

This model is informational. RPs are not required to implement these states or transitions internally. The normative requirements for RPs are defined by the lifecycle commands in Section 4. The model provides a shared vocabulary for reasoning about session state and the expected behavior of each command.

The IdP and RP manage sessions independently of each other. The federation protocol does not bind IdP session state to RP session state. §5.3. This model describes the RP-side view of the federated session.

section.t: The lifecycle defines four progressive levels of Identity Service control over RP sessions:

texttable.c: "Come back now and prove it with full authentication"

section.name: State Descriptions
section.t: Unauthenticated: No session exists for the subject at the RP. The subject has not yet authenticated or all prior authentication state has been terminated. This is the initial state and the return state after Terminated. §7.1

Established: The RP has received and successfully validated an assertion from the IdP. Prior to this state, the RP redirected the subject to the IdP; the IdP authenticated the subject (using an intent of Session Continuation, User Presence, Step-Up Authentication, or Forced Reauthentication depending on context — see Section 3.7) and issued an assertion (an OIDC ID Token or SAML <Assertion>). Upon receiving the assertion, the RP validates it (signature, issuer, audience, freshness), records the session authority (iss, sub, and optionally sid), establishes a local RP client session bound to the assertion, and MAY issue OAuth access tokens and refresh tokens to first-party clients. The subject MAY create API keys. These artifacts collectively form the subject's authentication state at the RP. If any validation step fails, the subject returns to Unauthenticated. §5–6, §3.1.2, §3.4, §7.1

Active: The subject has an established session and is accessing RP resources using the session, tokens, and API keys. The session authority is fixed for the lifetime of the session: the RP MUST NOT accept assertions from a different Identity Service to continue this session. The RP enforces session validity, token lifetime, and authorization policy. Token refresh operations extend API access without requiring reauthentication. §7.2
Expired: The subject's RP client sessions are no longer valid due to time-based expiry. Expiry may be triggered by:

list.t: Inactivity timeout: No subscriber activity within the configured timeout period §7.2
Absolute timeout: Maximum session duration reached regardless of activity §7.2

section.t: Tokens and API keys remain valid. The session authority is retained, so the RP redirects the subject to the same Identity Service that established the session without requiring IdP discovery. The subject returns to the Established state. The authentication intent depends on how the session expired:

list.t: Time-based expiry: The IdP may satisfy the request via Session Continuation, User Presence, Step-Up Authentication, or Forced Reauthentication depending on its policy and the RP's expressed requirements. This is the IdP's opportunity to periodically re-evaluate whether the subject should continue to have access.

Reestablish Session command: The Identity Service explicitly requires Forced Reauthentication. Session Continuation, User Presence, and Step-Up Authentication are NOT sufficient. The IdP re-evaluates policy, risk, device posture, account state, and conditional access rules before deciding whether to issue a new assertion. See Section 3.3 for Forced Reauthentication requirements.

section.t: Terminated: The subject's RP client session is terminated and the subject must re-authenticate through the Identity Service before regaining interactive access. This state is reached via two distinct triggers with different artifact scopes:

list.t: Logout (user, admin, policy, or system-initiated): The RP session is terminated. Tokens and API keys are typically preserved, as the subject may have active background processes. The Identity Service is given an opportunity to re-evaluate policy, risk, and account state before issuing a new assertion. See Section 2 for the definition of Logout.

Invalidate Access command (SL2): The most severe level of Identity Service control, indicating a security event. All authentication artifacts (sessions, tokens, and API keys) are invalidated or revoked. Prior authentication artifacts MUST NOT be trusted.

section.t: In both cases the session authority is cleared. The subject returns to the Unauthenticated state and, if the RP supports multiple Identity Services, may select a different Identity Service when establishing a new session. §7.1

texttable.c: Time-based; Session Continuation, Step-Up, or Forced Reauthentication permitted (SL1)
Subject cannot resume session; Forced Reauthentication required
Identity Service-initiated security operation; all artifacts invalidated (SL2)
Authentication intent depends on trigger (see Section 2)
Session authority cleared; subject may select a different IdP

section.name: Progressive IdP Control
section.t: The Identity Service has four progressive levels of control over RP sessions:

texttable.c: Session Continuation, User Presence, Step-Up, or Forced Reauthentication
MUST require new authentication ceremony; MAY use existing session context
Cleared; subject may select a different IdP
Cleared; subject may select a different IdP

section.name: Authentication Intents
section.t: When a Relying Party redirects a subject to the Identity Provider, the resulting authentication interaction falls into one of four intents. These intents are orthogonal to protocol mechanics and are derived from the RP's expressed requirements (e.g., prompt, max_age, acr_values) and the IdP's local policy and risk evaluation.

section.name: Session Continuation
section.t: Session Continuation occurs when a Relying Party requests authentication and the Identity Provider determines that an existing authentication session satisfies the RP's stated authentication freshness and assurance requirements.
In this intent, no new authentication event occurs.

section.name: Properties
section.t: When performing Session Continuation:

list.t: An existing IdP authentication session MUST exist and remain valid.
The IdP MUST NOT require the user to perform a new primary authentication ceremony.
The existing authentication context, including auth_time, acr, and amr, MUST be preserved.
New tokens MAY be issued to the RP.
The IdP MUST treat the request as a continuation of the existing authentication session, not as a reauthentication.

section.name: Typical Triggers
section.t: Session Continuation is commonly applicable when:

list.t: An RP session has expired or been terminated locally.
The user agent has restarted or lost RP cookies.
The RP has performed an RP-local logout.
The RP is re-establishing application state.

section.name: Protocol Expression
section.t: An RP requesting Session Continuation MUST NOT include prompt=login (OIDC) or ForceAuthn="true" (SAML). The RP MAY use prompt=none (OIDC) or IsPassive="true" (SAML) to require silent continuation. If no valid IdP session exists, the IdP returns an error rather than prompting the user. The RP also:

list.t: Omits max_age or supplies a value satisfied by the existing session.
Does not request higher assurance via acr_values.

section.name: IdP Behavior
section.t: If the IdP determines that the existing authentication session satisfies the RP's requirements, the IdP MUST perform Session Continuation.
The IdP MAY override Session Continuation and require additional authentication based on risk signals or local policy.

section.name: User Presence
section.t: User Presence occurs when the Relying Party requires the subject to actively confirm they are present at the session, without requiring a full primary authentication ceremony or an elevated assurance level.

In this intent, the subject performs a lightweight presence gesture. The existing authentication session is preserved, but the subject must actively interact to confirm presence. User Presence is stronger than Session Continuation (which requires no user interaction) but weaker than Step-Up Authentication (which elevates assurance) and Forced Reauthentication (which requires a full ceremony).

section.name: Properties
section.t: When performing User Presence:

list.t: An existing IdP authentication session MUST exist and remain valid.
The IdP MUST require the subject to perform an active presence gesture (e.g., touch a security key, complete a biometric scan, enter a PIN, or acknowledge a push notification).
The presence gesture MUST NOT constitute a full primary authentication ceremony.
The existing acr MUST be set to urn:ipsie:acr:presence in the issued assertion to reflect the presence confirmation.
The amr claim MUST reflect the specific gesture performed (e.g., hwk, fpt, pin).
auth_time MUST be updated to reflect the time of the presence confirmation.
New tokens MAY be issued to the RP.
The session identifier MUST remain the same.

section.name: Typical Triggers
section.t: User Presence is commonly applicable when:

list.t: The subject has been idle for a period that warrants a lightweight confirmation of presence.
A sensitive operation requires recent proof of presence without full reauthentication.
Risk signals (e.g., idle time, screen lock, location shift) suggest the user should confirm they are still at the device.
Regulatory or policy requirements mandate proof of presence at a specific interval without mandating full reauthentication.

section.name: Protocol Expression
section.t: An RP requesting User Presence requests a defined presence ACR value:

texttable.c: acr = urn:ipsie:acr:presence; amr reflects the gesture
AuthnContextClassRef in the assertion reflects the same value

section.t: The RP MUST NOT include prompt=login or ForceAuthn="true", as those require Forced Reauthentication. The RP MUST NOT include prompt=none or IsPassive="true", as those prohibit user interaction.
The RP MUST verify that the returned acr equals urn:ipsie:acr:presence (or higher) and that auth_time reflects the time of the presence confirmation.

section.name: IdP Behavior
section.t: When the RP requests acr_values="urn:ipsie:acr:presence":

list.t: The IdP MUST prompt the subject for a presence gesture if the existing session does not already satisfy urn:ipsie:acr:presence within the required timeframe.
The IdP MUST NOT silently reuse the existing session without a presence gesture (i.e., MUST NOT perform Session Continuation).
The IdP MUST NOT require a full primary authentication ceremony solely to satisfy a User Presence request.
The IdP MAY escalate to Step-Up Authentication or Forced Reauthentication based on risk signals or local policy.

section.name: Step-Up Authentication
section.t: Step-Up Authentication occurs when the Relying Party requires a higher level of assurance than is provided by the existing authentication session.
In this intent, the IdP performs additional authentication steps sufficient to satisfy the requested assurance level.

section.name: Properties
section.t: When performing Step-Up Authentication:

list.t: An existing IdP authentication session MUST exist.
The IdP MUST evaluate whether the current authentication context satisfies the requested assurance.
If the assurance is insufficient, the IdP MUST require additional authentication.
The IdP MAY reuse previously satisfied authentication factors.
The resulting authentication context MUST reflect the updated assurance, including updated acr, amr, and auth_time as appropriate.

section.name: Typical Triggers
section.t: Step-Up Authentication is commonly applicable when:

list.t: Accessing sensitive or privileged resources.
Performing high-risk transactions.
Responding to increased risk signals (e.g., device change, location change).

section.name: Protocol Expression
section.t: An RP requesting Step-Up Authentication typically:

list.t: Requests a higher assurance level using acr_values.
Optionally requests specific authentication methods via claims.

section.name: Forced Reauthentication
section.t: Forced Reauthentication occurs when the Relying Party explicitly requires a fresh authentication event, regardless of any existing authentication session at the IdP.
In this intent, the existing authentication session MUST NOT be reused.

section.name: Properties
section.t: When performing Forced Reauthentication:

list.t: Any existing authentication session MUST NOT satisfy the request.
The IdP MUST require a new primary authentication ceremony.
The resulting authentication context MUST have a new auth_time.
Previous authentication context values MUST NOT be relied upon.
The RP MUST verify that the IdP has issued a new session identifier (sid in OIDC, SessionIndex in SAML) and MUST NOT reuse the prior session identifier.

section.name: Typical Triggers
section.t: Forced Reauthentication is commonly applicable when:

list.t: The RP has received a Reestablish Session command from the IdP.
The RP has received an Invalidate Access command from the IdP.
An Identity Service-initiated logout or account recovery has occurred.
Regulatory or security policy mandates reauthentication.

section.name: Protocol Expression
section.t: An RP requesting Forced Reauthentication MUST:

texttable.c: Forces full authentication, disallows SSO session reuse

section.t: The RP MUST validate auth_time (OIDC) or AuthnInstant (SAML) to confirm that a new authentication occurred. The RP MUST verify that the session identifier (sid / SessionIndex) is different from the prior session. The RP SHOULD reject authentications that appear to reuse prior sessions.

texttable.c: Confirm subject is present at the device
Elevate assurance for a specific operation
Access revalidation. IdP re-evaluates policy, risk, and state
Reflects the specific gesture (e.g., hwk, fpt, pin)
New. MUST differ from prior session
New RP session, existing IdP session
New RP session, new IdP authentication
Validates presence gesture; session not re-established
Full policy evaluation: risk, device posture, conditional access, account state
RP (for presence-sensitive operations or idle confirmation)
RP (in response to IdP command or RP-local policy)

section.name: Command Requirements
section.t: Both lifecycle commands defined in this specification require the RP to trigger Forced Reauthentication when the subject next interacts with the RP. Session Continuation, User Presence, and Step-Up Authentication are NOT sufficient to satisfy either command.

texttable.c: The Identity Service must perform a full policy evaluation to determine whether to grant continued access. Reusing an existing session would bypass this evaluation.
All prior authentication artifacts are invalidated. A completely new authentication is required.

section.t: When no command has been received (for example, when the RP's local session has expired, cookies have been lost, or the RP has performed an RP-local logout), the RP MAY allow Session Continuation. In this case, the RP does not include prompt=login or ForceAuthn="true", and the IdP may satisfy the request from an existing authentication session.

section.name: Authentication Intent Requirements by Session State
section.t: The authentication intent used when the subject returns to the Established state depends on the prior session state and how it was reached.

texttable.c: Session Continuation, User Presence, Step-Up, or Forced Reauthentication
IdP session may still be valid; IdP re-evaluates on check-back; RP MAY request presence confirmation for sensitive operations
Identity Service explicitly requires full policy re-evaluation; RP MUST use prompt=login / ForceAuthn="true"; IdP MUST require new authentication ceremony
Session ended; subject must re-authenticate through the Identity Service
Security event; all prior artifacts are untrusted; full authentication required

section.name: Reestablish Session
section.t: An Identity Service command requiring the RP to expire all of the subject's RP client sessions and reestablish them through a full authentication at the Identity Service. The purpose of this command is access revalidation. It gives the Identity Service the opportunity to re-evaluate policy, risk, device posture, account state, and conditional access rules before allowing the subject to continue accessing the RP.

This command transitions the session to the Expired state and requires Forced Reauthentication. Session Continuation and Step-Up Authentication are not sufficient. This is the only behavioral difference from time-based session expiry: when triggered by the Reestablish Session command, the RP MUST require Forced Reauthentication rather than allowing Session Continuation.
Scope: All RP client sessions for the subject: browser cookie sessions, native-app session tokens, and any other interactive session state.

section.name: RP Requirements
section.t: When an RP receives this command, it MUST:

list.t: Suspend all RP client sessions for the subject (sessions are no longer accepted)
Invalidate all associated session identifiers (delete session cookies, revoke native-app session tokens)
Require Forced Reauthentication at the Identity Service (see Section 3.3)

section.t: The RP MUST NOT:

list.t: Silently re-establish the session using existing tokens, SSO cookies, or Session Continuation
Revoke OAuth access tokens or refresh tokens at the Authorization Server
Revoke API keys (service keys, personal access tokens, static bearer tokens)
Treat this as authorization revocation or change roles/permissions

section.name: Identity Service Requirements
section.t: When an Identity Service sends this command, it MAY:

list.t: Expire the IdP SSO session (deployment-dependent)

section.name: Invalidate Access
section.t: An Identity Service command requiring the RP to treat all existing authentication artifacts as untrusted, including sessions, access tokens, refresh tokens, and API keys. This command transitions the session to the Terminated state (see Section 2), which invalidates all artifacts and requires Forced Reauthentication. This is the most severe level of Identity Service control, indicating a security event.
Scope: All prior authentication state: sessions, tokens, and API keys.

section.name: RP Requirements
section.t: When an RP receives this command, it MUST:

list.t: Terminate all RP client sessions for the subject (sessions are no longer accepted)
Invalidate all associated session identifiers (delete session cookies, revoke native-app session tokens)
Invalidate all existing access tokens for the subject
Invalidate all existing refresh tokens for the subject
Revoke all API keys for the subject (service keys, personal access tokens, static bearer tokens)
Require Forced Reauthentication at the Identity Service (see Section 3.3)
Reject any subsequent use of tokens or API keys that were issued before this command was received

section.t: The RP MUST NOT:

list.t: Accept tokens or API keys that were issued before the invalidation event
Treat this as authorization revocation or change roles/permissions

section.name: Identity Service Requirements
section.t: When an Identity Service sends this command, it MUST:

list.t: Invalidate the IdP SSO session
Revoke refresh tokens for the subject at the Authorization Server
Invalidate all access tokens for the subject (e.g., via revocation, revocation lists, or CAEP events to Resource Servers)

Notify Resource Servers of token invalidation via applicable mechanisms (e.g., token introspection status, revocation lists, or CAEP/SSF events) so that Resource Servers can detect and reject invalidated tokens

section.name: CAEP Events (SL3)
section.t: At SL3, the RP SHOULD publish CAEP events after processing lifecycle commands. This enables downstream Resource Servers and other participants in the SSF stream to stop accepting artifacts for the subject without waiting for token expiry or polling for revocation status.

section.name: Reestablish Session Events
section.t: After processing a Reestablish Session command, the RP SHOULD publish:

texttable.c: Notify the ecosystem that the subject's RP client session has been expired

section.t: The RP SHOULD include the following claims in the session-revoked event:

list.t: sub: The subject whose session was expired
reason_admin: Indicate that session reestablishment was requested (e.g., "Session reestablishment required by Identity Service")
event_timestamp: The time at which the RP expired the session

section.t: The RP SHOULD NOT publish credential-change events for Reestablish Session, as tokens and API keys are unaffected.

section.name: Invalidate Access Events
section.t: After processing an Invalidate Access command, the RP SHOULD publish an access_revoked event. This specification proposes access_revoked as a new CAEP event type to represent the full scope of the Invalidate Access command: all sessions terminated, all tokens invalidated, and all API keys revoked atomically. A single event is preferable to composing session-revoked and multiple credential-change events because it allows receivers to understand the complete revocation atomically without correlating multiple signals.

Status: This event type is a proposed extension to the CAEP specification and is not yet formally registered. Implementers should treat the URI and claim structure as subject to change pending registration.

texttable.c: The subject whose access was revoked (format: iss_sub or opaque)
The time at which the RP completed the revocation
Who triggered the revocation: policy (Identity Service command), admin, or system
Human-readable reason (e.g., "Invalidate Access command received from Identity Service")

section.t: Fallback: Until access_revoked is formally registered, RPs MAY publish session-revoked (with reason_admin indicating full access revocation) together with credential-change (revoke) events as a fallback. Receivers that support access_revoked MUST treat it as equivalent to receiving both signals simultaneously.

section.name: Atomicity
section.t: Each command MUST either complete fully or fail. Partial completion is not acceptable. The RP MUST NOT report success if any required step has not been performed.

If the RP requires asynchronous processing to complete a command (e.g., AS-side token revocation involves an external call), the RP MUST use a mechanism that supports deferred completion. The OP Commands specification supports asynchronous command processing; where this mechanism is not available, this specification proposes that implementations adopt an equivalent async response model (e.g., returning an accepted status and providing a callback or polling mechanism for completion confirmation). The RP MUST NOT report success before all steps are complete.
If any step fails (e.g., AS is unreachable for token revocation), the RP MUST report failure. The Identity Service SHOULD retry failed commands.

section.name: Idempotency
section.t: Commands MUST be idempotent. If the RP receives the same command multiple times (e.g., due to IdP retry after a network failure), it MUST process the command and report success, even if the resulting state has already been achieved by a prior command.
The RP MAY use the jti claim (when present) to detect duplicate commands for logging purposes, but MUST NOT reject a command solely because a command with the same jti was previously processed.

section.name: Command Ordering
section.t: Invalidate Access is a strict superset of Reestablish Session. It includes all session invalidation steps plus token invalidation and API key revocation. In the session lifecycle model, Reestablish Session transitions to the Expired state while Invalidate Access transitions to the Terminated state (see Section 2.4).
If both commands are received for the same subject:

list.t: Reestablish Session after Invalidate Access: The RP MUST succeed. The session is already in the Terminated state. All artifacts are invalidated. No further action is needed.

Invalidate Access after Reestablish Session: The RP MUST process the full Invalidate Access command. The session transitions from the Expired state to the Terminated state. Sessions are already expired, but the RP must additionally invalidate tokens and revoke API keys.

section.t: In general, the RP SHOULD apply each command to the current state of the subject's artifacts. A command succeeds if the resulting state defined in Sections 4.1.3 or 4.2.3 is achieved, regardless of what prior state existed.

section.name: Protocol Mappings
section.t: A protocol maps to a command only if it can fully complete that command. Protocols that cover only part of a command's scope (e.g., token revocation without session invalidation) cannot fulfill a command on their own and are listed as composition components where applicable.

section.name: Completeness Requirement
section.t: Each command defines a complete resulting state (Sections 4.1.3 and 4.2.3). A protocol implementation MUST achieve the full resulting state of a command to claim support for that command. Partial fulfillment is not sufficient.

Implication: It is acceptable for a protocol to support only one of the two commands. For example, OIDC Back-Channel Logout can fully complete "Reestablish Session" but cannot on its own complete "Invalidate Access" (it does not revoke tokens). Similarly, OAuth Token Revocation revokes tokens but does not expire RP client sessions, so it cannot complete either command alone.

section.name: Reestablish Session: Protocol Mappings
section.t: The following protocols can fully complete the Reestablish Session command because they expire or terminate the RP client session and require the RP to reestablish it through a full authentication at the Identity Service.

Note on Logout protocols (BCL, FCL, SAML SLO): These protocols implement the Logout trigger, transitioning the session to the Terminated state (tokens preserved). Because Terminated requires Forced Reauthentication through the Identity Service, Logout gives the Identity Service the same access-revalidation opportunity as the Reestablish Session command. The IdP can re-evaluate policy, risk, device posture, and account state before issuing a new assertion. This is why Logout protocols satisfy the Reestablish Session command contract, even though they terminate rather than mark the session Invalid.

section.name: OIDC Back-Channel Logout (RECOMMENDED)

texttable.c: IdP sends a Logout Token to the RP's registered backchannel_logout_uri
sub claim and/or sid (session ID) claim
Terminate (Logout transition) the RP client session(s) matching sub/sid; do NOT revoke OAuth tokens
Yes — satisfies Reestablish Session via Logout (see note above)

section.t: See Appendix B for RP implementation steps.

section.name: OIDC Front-Channel Logout (ACCEPTABLE)

texttable.c: IdP renders an iframe pointing to the RP's frontchannel_logout_uri
iss and sid (if session management supported)
Terminate (Logout transition) the RP session; clear session cookies and expire server-side session state; do NOT revoke OAuth tokens
Conditionally — only when browser is active and iframes/cookies are not blocked; satisfies Reestablish Session via Logout (see note above)

section.t: Limitations: Fails if browser is closed, third-party cookies are blocked, or iframes are suppressed. NOT RECOMMENDED as sole mechanism.

section.name: SAML 2.0 Single Logout (ACCEPTABLE)
section.t: Specification: Section 4.4

texttable.c: Terminate (Logout transition) the RP client session matching the NameID/SessionIndex; do NOT revoke OAuth tokens; respond with <LogoutResponse>
Yes (back-channel SOAP) / Conditionally (front-channel) — satisfies Reestablish Session via Logout (see note above)

section.t: Limitations: Front-channel binding is browser-dependent and fragile in multi-SP deployments. SOAP back-channel is more reliable but less widely implemented.
See Appendix B for SP implementation steps (back-channel SOAP binding).

section.name: OpenID Provider Commands: reestablish (PROPOSED)
section.t: Specification: (proposed extension — see Appendix C)

This specification proposes a new OP Command type reestablish as an extension to . The reestablish command type is not yet registered in the OP Commands specification; see Appendix C for the proposed formal registration. When adopted, it maps directly to the Reestablish Session lifecycle command.

texttable.c: Identity Service sends a Command Token to the RP's registered command endpoint
JWT with typ: command+jwt, signed with Identity Service signing keys
iss, aud, client_id, iat, exp, jti, command, tenant, sub
Suspend all RP client sessions for the subject; do NOT revoke OAuth tokens; require Forced Reauthentication at Identity Service for session reestablishment
Yes — fully satisfies Reestablish Session when adopted

section.t: See Appendix B for RP implementation steps.

section.name: OpenID Provider Commands: invalidate (RECOMMENDED)
section.t: The OP Command type invalidate maps to the Invalidate Access lifecycle command, transitioning the session to the Terminated state. The invalidate command is a strict superset of the reestablish command. It includes all session invalidation steps plus token invalidation and API key revocation. When the Identity Service sends invalidate, it signals that all prior authentication artifacts for the subject must be treated as untrusted.

texttable.c: Identity Service sends a Command Token to the RP's registered command endpoint
JWT with typ: command+jwt, signed with Identity Service signing keys
iss, aud, client_id, iat, exp, jti, command, tenant, sub
Invalidate RP client session, invalidate all existing access and refresh tokens, revoke all API keys for the subject, require reauthentication

section.t: See Appendix B for RP implementation steps. See Section 7 for self-contained JWT access token considerations.

section.name: Protocol Comparison
section.t: The following table compares the scope of each protocol when used for the Invalidate Access command.
When not using OP Commands (invalidate), implementations MUST compose protocols to achieve full coverage:

c.strong: RP session + token invalidation + API key revocation

texttable.c: OIDC Back-Channel Logout / SAML SLO (session only; RP must additionally invalidate tokens and revoke API keys)
OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation or Global Token Revocation

section.name: Supplementary Protocols
section.t: The following protocols may be used as supplementary components when OP Commands (invalidate) is not available, or for additional ecosystem-wide enforcement.

texttable.c: IdP (acting as or coordinating with the AS) revokes tokens
Revokes specified token; AS SHOULD also invalidate related tokens (e.g., revoking a refresh token invalidates its access tokens)
Revoke all refresh tokens for the subject
No — does not invalidate RP client sessions
IdP requests revocation of all tokens for a subject
All access tokens and refresh tokens for the subject at the AS
Single request revokes all tokens vs. per-token revocation
No — does not invalidate RP client sessions
Informational by default; requires enforcement profile for mandatory RP enforcement
No — does not invalidate sessions or revoke tokens

section.t: MUST NOT be the sole mechanism for this command. Useful as supplementary broadcast.

section.name: Protocol Mapping Summary
section.t: Both commands are REQUIRED at SL2. The following table summarizes which command each protocol can fully complete.

texttable.c: PROPOSED — completes command when adopted (see Appendix C)
RECOMMENDED — completes command (sessions + tokens + API keys)
Session layer only; must compose with token revocation and API key revocation
Session layer only; must compose with token revocation and API key revocation
Session layer only; must compose with token revocation and API key revocation
Token layer only; must compose with session invalidation
Token layer only; must compose with session invalidation
PROPOSED — completes command via session-revoked when adopted (see Section 4.1.4)
PROPOSED — completes command via access_revoked when adopted (see Section 4.2.4)

section.t: Note on Shared Signals: If both CAEP proposals are adopted — session-revoked for Reestablish Session and access_revoked for Invalidate Access — the Shared Signals Framework can serve as the delivery mechanism for both lifecycle commands. This enables a single SSF stream to carry the full range of Identity Service-initiated session lifecycle events to RPs.

section.name: Recommended Protocol Combinations
section.t: Implementations conforming to SL2 MUST support at least one protocol or protocol combination that fully completes each command.

The SSO protocol in use determines which logout protocol is applicable. OIDC Back-Channel Logout and SAML 2.0 Single Logout are mutually exclusive — an RP uses the logout protocol that matches its SSO federation protocol. SAML SLO is not a fallback for BCL; they serve the same role in their respective protocol stacks.

section.name: Reestablish Session (SL2 REQUIRED)
section.t: A single protocol can fully complete this command.
If SSO is OIDC (RECOMMENDED): - OIDC Back-Channel Logout
If SSO is SAML (ACCEPTABLE): - SAML 2.0 SLO (back-channel SOAP binding)

When Adopted (RECOMMENDED — see Appendix C and Section 4.1.4): - OP Commands (reestablish): completes the command in a single protocol exchange, independent of SSO protocol - Shared Signals (CAEP session-revoked): 1:1 equivalent to OP Commands (reestablish) via SSF delivery; independent of SSO protocol; preferred when an SSF stream is already established

section.name: Invalidate Access (SL2 REQUIRED)
section.t: Primary (RECOMMENDED): - OP Commands (invalidate): completes the command in a single protocol exchange, independent of SSO protocol

When Adopted (RECOMMENDED — see Section 4.2.4): - Shared Signals (CAEP access_revoked): 1:1 equivalent to OP Commands (invalidate) via SSF delivery; independent of SSO protocol; preferred when an SSF stream is already established. If both reestablish and access_revoked proposals are adopted, a single SSF stream covers both commands.

When neither OP Commands nor Shared Signals access_revoked is available, implementations MUST compose protocols to achieve full coverage. The session layer protocol depends on the SSO protocol in use:

texttable.c: OAuth Token Revocation (RFC 7009) or OAuth Global Token Revocation
OAuth Token Revocation (RFC 7009) or OAuth Global Token Revocation

section.name: Self-Contained JWT Access Token Considerations
section.t: Self-contained JWT access tokens present a unique challenge for "Invalidate Access" because they are validated locally by the Resource Server without contacting the Authorization Server. If the RP cannot invalidate these tokens on demand, the token lifetime becomes the maximum exposure window during which an invalidated token may still be accepted.

section.name: On-Demand Invalidation
section.t: RPs that can invalidate self-contained access tokens immediately upon receiving an Invalidate Access command (for example, via revocation lists, status lists , or event-driven invalidation (CAEP/SSF)) are not subject to the maximum TTL constraints in Section 7.2.

texttable.c: RS must fetch and check list (operational complexity)

section.t: RPs that implement on-demand invalidation MUST invalidate self-contained access tokens within an implementation-defined latency appropriate to the deployment's risk tolerance. In practice, invalidation SHOULD complete within seconds of receiving the command.

section.name: Maximum Token Lifetime
section.t: When the RP cannot invalidate self-contained access tokens on demand, the token lifetime is the sole control bounding the exposure window. In this case, self-contained access tokens MUST comply with the following maximum lifetime constraints:

texttable.c: Bounds the exposure window to an acceptable duration for general enterprise use
Minimizes the exposure window for environments requiring continuous access evaluation

section.t: The exp claim in a self-contained access token MUST NOT exceed the maximum TTL for the applicable IPSIE level, measured from the iat claim. When the RP operates its own Authorization Server, that Authorization Server MUST enforce these limits at token issuance.
For "Invalidate Access," implementers SHOULD implement on-demand invalidation (Section 7.1) rather than relying solely on token expiry.

list.t: Transport security: All protocol messages MUST use TLS 1.2 or higher.

Message integrity: Lifecycle commands MUST be authenticated (signed, MAC'd, or delivered over an authenticated channel). For OP Commands, the Command Token MUST be a signed JWT verified against the Identity Service's JWKS.
Replay protection: Lifecycle commands MUST include a jti (JWT ID) claim and an exp claim. RPs SHOULD reject commands with expired exp or duplicate jti values within a reasonable window.

Sender authorization: RPs MUST verify that lifecycle commands originate from a trusted Identity Service (e.g., by validating the iss claim against known Identity Service metadata and verifying the signature against the Identity Service's JWKS).
Command endpoint protection: RP command endpoints MUST be protected against unauthorized access. Endpoints SHOULD implement rate limiting to reduce the risk of denial-of-service via command flooding.

Fail-secure: When a command type is unknown or cannot be parsed, RPs SHOULD default to the more restrictive behavior (treat as Invalidate Access). Note that this fail-secure behavior could itself be a denial-of-service vector if an attacker can submit malformed commands; RPs MUST enforce sender authorization before applying fail-secure defaults.

Enforcement gaps: Browser-dependent mechanisms (Front-Channel Logout, front-channel SAML SLO) may fail silently if the browser is closed or third-party cookies are blocked. Implementers SHOULD prefer back-channel mechanisms for security-critical commands.

section.name: Reference Deployment Model
section.t: The following diagram illustrates a common SaaS deployment where the Application acts as an RP to the enterprise IdP but also operates its own first-party Authorization Server that issues access tokens and refresh tokens to its own first-party clients (web app, mobile app, CLI).
In this model, the SaaS Application is both:

list.t: A Relying Party (RP) that depends on the enterprise IdP for user authentication via SSO
A first-party Authorization Server that issues its own OAuth access tokens and refresh tokens to its own clients (web app, mobile app, CLI)

section.t: The authentication artifacts managed by the SaaS Application include:

texttable.c: Browser cookie sessions, native-app session tokens
Short-lived tokens issued to 1st-party clients for API access
Long-lived tokens used by 1st-party clients to obtain new access tokens
Service keys, PATs, and static bearer tokens issued to users

section.name: Command Effects on This Deployment
section.t: Reestablish Session: IdP sends reestablish:

figure.artwork: IdP --reestablish--> SaaS Application (RP) | +-- RP client sessions ......... EXPIRE +-- Access tokens .............. unchanged +-- Refresh tokens ............. unchanged +-- API keys ................... unchanged

section.t: All of the user's interactive sessions are expired. First-party clients holding valid access tokens or refresh tokens continue to operate. Background API integrations using API keys are unaffected. The user must complete a full authentication at the IdP, where the IdP re-evaluates policy, risk, and state, to establish a new session.
Invalidate Access: IdP sends invalidate:

figure.artwork: IdP --invalidate--> SaaS Application (RP) | +-- RP client sessions ......... INVALIDATE +-- Access tokens .............. INVALIDATE +-- Refresh tokens ............. INVALIDATE +-- API keys ................... REVOKE | | 1st-Party AS +-- Revoke refresh tokens at AS +-- Revoke/invalidate access tokens at AS

section.t: All authentication artifacts for the subject are invalidated or revoked. Access tokens held by first-party clients will be invalid on next use. Refresh token rotation will fail. API key-based integrations will stop functioning. The user and all automated integrations must reauthenticate at the IdP and obtain new credentials.

Note on deployment: In this deployment, the SaaS Application is both the RP and the AS. When the RP receives an OP Commands invalidate command, it invalidates sessions, tokens, and API keys in a single internal operation. When the RP and AS are separate entities, the RP is still responsible for invalidating all authentication artifacts within its domain upon receiving the command.

section.name: Protocol Implementation Details
section.t: This appendix provides detailed RP implementation steps for each protocol mapping defined in Section 5. These steps are informational and intended to guide implementers.

list.t: Validate the Logout Token signature against Identity Service JWKS
Verify iss, aud, iat, and events claims
Look up local session(s) by sub and/or sid
Terminate matching RP client sessions (Logout transition; sessions are no longer accepted; do NOT revoke OAuth tokens)
On next user interaction, trigger Forced Reauthentication (see Section 3.3)

section.name: SAML 2.0 Single Logout: SP Implementation (Back-Channel SOAP)

list.t: Validate <LogoutRequest> signature
Verify Issuer, Destination, NameID
Look up local session by NameID and SessionIndex
Terminate matching session (Logout transition; session is no longer accepted; do NOT revoke OAuth tokens)
Return <LogoutResponse> with Success status
On next user interaction, trigger Forced Reauthentication (see Section 3.3)

section.name: OpenID Provider Commands reestablish: RP Implementation
section.t: Note: The reestablish command type is a proposed extension to . See Appendix C.

list.t: Validate Command Token signature against Identity Service JWKS
Verify typ is command+jwt
Verify iss, aud, iat, exp, jti, and command claims
Confirm command value is reestablish
Look up all sessions by sub (and tenant if applicable)
Expire all matching RP client sessions (sessions are no longer accepted)
Return success response
On next user interaction, trigger Forced Reauthentication (see Section 3.3)

section.name: OpenID Provider Commands invalidate: RP Implementation

list.t: Validate Command Token signature against Identity Service JWKS
Verify typ is command+jwt
Verify iss, aud, iat, exp, jti, and command claims
Confirm command value is invalidate
Look up all sessions by sub (and tenant if applicable)
Terminate all matching RP client sessions (sessions are no longer accepted)
Invalidate all existing access tokens for the subject
Invalidate all existing refresh tokens for the subject
Revoke all API keys for the subject (service keys, personal access tokens, static bearer tokens)
Return success response
On next user interaction, trigger Forced Reauthentication (see Section 3.3)

section.t: Note: Because invalidate is a superset of reestablish, any RP that implements invalidate inherently satisfies the Reestablish Session command as well. The RP is responsible for invalidating all authentication artifacts within its domain, including any tokens issued by its own Authorization Server. See Section 7 for self-contained JWT access token considerations.

section.name: Suggested Protocol Extensions
section.t: The following extensions would improve the ability to implement these commands with clear semantics and guaranteed enforcement. These are proposals for future standardization work submitted to the relevant working groups.

section.name: OpenID Provider Commands: reestablish Command Registration
section.t: Problem: The OP Commands specification () defines invalidate but does not define a session reestablishment command. The invalidate command implies full authentication state revocation, which is too broad for the Reestablish Session use case where the Identity Service wants to revalidate access without invalidating tokens and API keys.
Proposed Registration: Register reestablish as a new OP Command type in .

texttable.c: Require the RP to expire the subject's sessions and reestablish them through a full authentication at the Identity Service. The Identity Service re-evaluates policy, risk, and state to determine whether to grant continued access. The RP MUST NOT revoke OAuth tokens or API keys.
iss, aud, client_id, iat, exp, jti, command, tenant, sub

section.t: The invalidate command is a strict superset of reestablish. It performs all reestablish steps plus token invalidation and API key revocation.

The RP MUST treat reestablish and invalidate as distinct commands with different scopes. Receiving reestablish MUST NOT trigger token invalidation; receiving invalidate MUST perform all reestablish steps and additionally invalidate tokens and revoke API keys.

section.name: CAEP: Enforcement Profile for Session Lifecycle
section.t: Problem: CAEP events are informational by default. An Identity Service cannot mandate that an RP act on a session-revoked event.
Suggested Extension: Define an enforcement profile that:

list.t: Maps CAEP event types to the commands defined in this specification
Requires the receiver to enforce the mapped command
Requires the receiver to report enforcement status

texttable.c: MUST terminate RP session (tokens preserved); Forced Reauthentication required
MUST expire RP session and require reestablishment with Forced Reauthentication
MUST terminate session, invalidate tokens, and revoke API keys
MUST terminate session, invalidate tokens, and revoke API keys
MUST terminate session, invalidate tokens, and revoke API keys; preferred over composing session-revoked + credential-change

section.t: Note on access-revoked: This event type is a proposed CAEP extension defined in Section 4.2.4. Receivers that recognize access-revoked MUST treat it as equivalent to session-revoked (reason: policy-violation) combined with credential-change (change type: revoke) for all artifact types.

Note on credential-change mapping: Only credential-change events with a change type of revoke map to Invalidate Access. Routine credential changes (e.g., password updates or MFA device additions with change type create or update) do NOT mandate this command; the Identity Service's policy determines whether such events warrant access revalidation.
